claims.text: Depositing a thin silicon-based ceramic coating on boride components will improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion during hot-dip aluminum plating.
Conventionally manufactured boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment are directly exposed to molten aluminum without an engineered surface barrier.
A silicon nitride or silicon oxide layer can serve as the proposed silicon-based ceramic coating.
Exposure of the silicon-based coating to molten aluminum may form a stable alumina or aluminosilicate interfacial layer.
The resulting alumina or aluminosilicate interfacial layer acts as a diffusion barrier.
At high temperature, the silicon-based coating reacts to produce a protective interfacial layer.
The protective interfacial layer limits direct contact between molten aluminum and the boride substrate.
The protective interfacial layer limits diffusion of molten aluminum into the boride substrate.
Limiting contact and diffusion retards corrosion of the boride component.
Coated boride components will exhibit lower corrosion rates and less degradation than otherwise comparable uncoated components.
The coating may improve durability by 20–30% under standard operating conditions.
The coating will remain effective during elevated-temperature, prolonged molten-aluminum exposure if thermal cycling and chemical conditions remain within its stability limits.
Extreme thermal cycling or overly prolonged exposure may degrade the coating and reduce its efficacy.
Coated and uncoated, otherwise identical boride components should be exposed under identical hot-dip aluminum-plating conditions for a controlled comparison.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in weight loss and improved interfacial integrity in the coated group would falsify the hypothesis.
